summary: Proposes using DTLS to protect DNS queries and responses from passive listeners and some active attacks, while keeping latency low. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Putting DNS questions in sealed envelopes so snoops cannot read them, without slowing replies much.

subtitle: Wrapping DNS queries in DTLS over UDP port 853 so eavesdroppers cannot read them, as an experimental backup to DNS over TLS.

tldr.problem: DNS queries and responses are normally unencrypted, so anyone on the path can see which domains a host wants to reach.
tldr.mechanism: DNS messages are carried unchanged inside a DTLS session on UDP port 853, with the client starting a normal DTLS handshake and authenticating the server.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental RFC, written mainly as a backup in case the TLS-based approach of RFC 7858 runs into problems when deployed.

facts.label: Minimum probe interval
facts.value: 15 minutes (SHOULD NOT be more often than 24 hours)

today: RFC 8094 is an Experimental RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself describes it mainly as a backup to DNS over TLS (RFC 7858), to be judged by implementation and interoperability testing.

sections.title: Why Encrypt DNS Over DTLS
sections.content:
DNS queries and responses are normally exchanged unencrypted, so they are vulnerable to eavesdropping. An eavesdropper can learn which domains a host wants to access, which is a privacy leak. DNS over DTLS gives confidential DNS communication between stub resolvers and recursive resolvers, stub resolvers and forwarders, and forwarders and recursive resolvers. It does not change the format of DNS messages.

The biggest privacy gain is protecting the link between the end user's machine and its caching resolver. The RFC names two motivations: TCP suffers from head-of-line blocking, where one lost packet holds back everything behind it, and DTLS over UDP does not. DTLS session resumption also takes one round trip, while TLS resumption can start only after the TCP handshake.
sections.eli5: Plain DNS is like a postcard that anyone along the way can read. DTLS puts it in a sealed envelope, and because it uses the fast kind of mail, one lost envelope does not hold up the others.

sections.title: Relationship to TCP, TLS and DNSSEC
sections.content:
This document covers only UDP. DNS over TCP can be protected with TLS as described in RFC 7858. DNS over DTLS alone cannot give privacy in every case, for example when the DTLS record would be larger than the path MTU and the server has to send a truncated response. So clients and servers that implement DNS over DTLS MUST also implement DNS over TLS, to serve clients that want Strict Privacy.

DNSSEC checks that records are genuine but gives no privacy. DNS over DTLS works together with DNSSEC and does not replace it.

The RFC says the DPRIVE working group considered this an option in case the TLS approach had deployment issues. At the time of writing, RFC 7858 was expected to be what gets deployed, so this specification is mainly a backup.
sections.eli5: This is the spare plan. The main plan uses a different kind of sealed envelope, and this one is kept ready in case the main plan has trouble.

sections.title: Sessions, Handshake and Authentication
sections.content:
By default DNS over DTLS MUST run over UDP port 853. A client finds out whether a server supports it by sending a DTLS ClientHello to port 853. A different port may be used by mutual agreement, but it MUST NOT be port 53, to avoid complications and to reduce the risk of downgrade attacks.

A server without DTLS support simply does not answer. The client SHOULD retransmit the ClientHello and give up after 15 seconds. It may probe again later, but SHOULD NOT do so more often than every 24 hours and MUST NOT do so more often than every 15 minutes.

Port 853 is for encrypted traffic only. Clients MUST NOT send, and servers MUST NOT answer, cleartext DNS on any port used for DNS over DTLS, even after a failed handshake.

Once the handshake succeeds, DNS messages are sent as ordinary DTLS application data, and one session can carry many queries and responses. Clients MUST minimize concurrent sessions to a server, and one session per client/server pair is RECOMMENDED. When idle, a server MUST send a DTLS fatal alert and destroy its state; the RFC recommends an idle time of several seconds and not less than a second, but specifies no value.

Authentication follows the handshake of RFC 6347 and the best practices of RFC 7525. Encryption also gives integrity protection, so on-path attackers cannot simply inject bogus responses. To resist attackers pretending to be the server, the client MUST authenticate the server using the mechanisms in the separate DNS-over-(D)TLS profile document; this RFC proposes no new authentication ideas.
sections.eli5: You knock on a special door (number 853) and, if someone answers, you whisper through it. If nobody answers, you try again for a bit, then give up and check back much later. Only secret talk is allowed at that door.

sections.title: Performance and Path MTU
sections.content:
Latency matters for DNS, so the RFC suggests ways to shrink the handshake. Clients and servers can use raw public keys (RFC 7250) or the Cached Information Extension (RFC 7924) to avoid sending a certificate that can be several kilobytes. TLS False Start (RFC 7918) can save round trips, and session resumption without server state (RFC 5077) removes the need to re-establish the session for later queries.

Responses can arrive out of order, so clients MUST match each response to an outstanding query on the same DTLS connection using the DNS Message ID, and the QNAME, QCLASS and QTYPE when a question section is present.

DTLS adds at least 13 octets of header plus cipher and authentication overhead to every message. Both sides MUST support EDNS0 (RFC 6891). If the path MTU is unknown, an IP MTU of 1280 bytes SHOULD be assumed. Each DTLS record MUST fit in a single datagram, and if a response would not fit, the server MUST send one that does and set the TC (truncated) bit. A client using Strict Privacy then MUST retry only over an encrypted transport such as DNS over TLS.
sections.eli5: The sealed envelope is a bit heavier, so the RFC shows ways to make the first hello shorter. If an answer is too big for one envelope, the server says so, and the client asks again another safe way.

sections.title: Anycast and Usage Profiles
sections.content:
DNS servers are often reached through anycast addresses. If routing changes, a packet can land on a server that has no cryptographic context for it. A server SHOULD then send a DTLS fatal alert to push the client to handshake again. Because an unauthenticated alert might be spoofed, the client SHOULD keep retransmitting its packet and at the same time SHOULD start DTLS session resumption, then close the other session once an authenticated response arrives on one of them.

Two usage profiles, Strict and Opportunistic, are defined in the separate profile document. The order of preference is: encrypted messages with an authenticated server, then encrypted messages with an unauthenticated server, then plaintext.
sections.eli5: Sometimes your question lands at a different helper who does not know your secret code. That helper tells you to start over, and you do so while still keeping your first try going, just in case the message was fake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DTLS must be used with a ciphersuite that offers confidentiality, and the guidance in RFC 7525 MUST be followed. The client SHOULD use OCSP stapling to check the server certificate's revocation status. Clients that remember which servers support DTLS can detect downgrade attacks.

ICMP errors cannot be authenticated, so they should be treated as soft errors. A response to a query sent over DTLS MUST be accepted only if it arrives over the same DTLS connection, which the RFC says mitigates all attacks described in RFC 5452.

A malicious client could start many handshakes. Because clients are not uniquely identified, a server needs to mitigate this, for example by rate limiting handshakes from a subnet.
sections.eli5: Keep using strong locks, only believe answers that come through your own sealed channel, and watch out for someone knocking on the door thousands of times to wear the server out.
